records.note: Tetrahedron {3,3}: 4 triangular faces, 3 at each vertex. The self-dual Platonic solid; the finite (1/p+1/q>1/2) counterpart of a regular {p,q} tiling.
Cube {4,3}: 6 square faces, 3 at each vertex. Dual of the octahedron.
Octahedron {3,4}: 8 triangular faces, 4 at each vertex. Dual of the cube.
Dodecahedron {5,3}: 12 pentagonal faces, 3 at each vertex. Dual of the icosahedron.
Icosahedron {3,5}: 20 triangular faces, 5 at each vertex. Dual of the dodecahedron.
Truncated tetrahedron 3.6.6: 4 triangles + 4 hexagons. The tetrahedron with its corners cut to one-third depth.
Cuboctahedron 3.4.3.4: 8 triangles + 6 squares. The rectification of the cube (and octahedron); its vertices are the cube's edge midpoints.
Truncated cube 3.8.8: 8 triangles + 6 octagons. The cube with its 8 corners cut off.
Truncated octahedron 4.6.6: 6 squares + 8 hexagons. The only Archimedean solid that also tiles 3-space by translation (the permutohedron).
Rhombicuboctahedron 3.4.4.4: 8 triangles + 18 squares. The cube's faces pushed out, the gaps filled with squares (cantellation).
Truncated cuboctahedron 4.6.8: 12 squares + 8 hexagons + 6 octagons. Also called the great rhombicuboctahedron.
Snub cube 3.3.3.3.4: 32 triangles + 6 squares. A chiral solid — shown here in one of its two mirror-image forms.
Icosidodecahedron 3.5.3.5: 20 triangles + 12 pentagons. The rectification of the icosahedron (and dodecahedron).
Truncated dodecahedron 3.10.10: 20 triangles + 12 decagons. The dodecahedron with its corners cut off.
Truncated icosahedron 5.6.6: 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons. The soccer-ball / buckyball shape.
Rhombicosidodecahedron 3.4.5.4: 20 triangles + 30 squares + 12 pentagons. The cantellation of the dodecahedron.
Truncated icosidodecahedron 4.6.10: 30 squares + 20 hexagons + 12 decagons. The largest Archimedean solid (120 vertices); also called the great rhombicosidodecahedron.
Snub dodecahedron 3.3.3.3.5: 80 triangles + 12 pentagons. A chiral solid — shown here in one of its two mirror-image forms.
Triangular prism (4.4.3): 2 triangles + 3 squares. The simplest prism; a regular n-gonal prism is inscribable for every n.
Pentagonal prism (4.4.5): 2 pentagons + 5 squares.
Hexagonal prism (4.4.6): 2 hexagons + 6 squares.
Octagonal prism (4.4.8): 2 octagons + 8 squares.
Decagonal prism (4.4.10): 2 decagons + 10 squares.
Square antiprism (3.3.3.4): 2 squares + 8 triangles. The n-gonal antiprism is inscribable for every n.
Pentagonal antiprism (3.3.3.5): 2 pentagons + 10 triangles.
Hexagonal antiprism (3.3.3.6): 2 hexagons + 12 triangles.
Octagonal antiprism (3.3.3.8): 2 octagons + 16 triangles.
Decagonal antiprism (3.3.3.10): 2 decagons + 20 triangles.
Triangular orthobicupola (Johnson solid J27): 8 triangles + 6 squares. The 2-orbit “ortho” twin of the cuboctahedron — same faces, but with adjacent-square 3.3.4.4 vertices the cuboctahedron lacks.

Pseudo-rhombicuboctahedron / elongated square gyrobicupola (Johnson solid J37): every vertex 3.4.4.4 yet not vertex-transitive — two orbits, one square cupola rotated 45°. The classic locally-but-not-globally-uniform solid.
Tridiminished icosahedron (Johnson solid J63): 5 triangles + 3 pentagons. The icosahedron with three pentagonal pyramids removed; remaining vertices stay on the icosahedron's circumsphere.
Diminished icosahedron / gyroelongated pentagonal pyramid (Johnson solid J11): 15 triangles + 1 pentagon. The icosahedron with one pentagonal pyramid removed.
Elongated square cupola (Johnson solid J19): 4 triangles + 13 squares + 1 octagon. Half of the rhombicuboctahedron (a square cupola on an octagonal prism); inscribable in the same sphere.
Pentagonal orthobirotunda (Johnson solid J34): 20 triangles + 12 pentagons. The 2-orbit ortho twin of the icosidodecahedron (one rotunda rotated 36°), with 3.3.5.5 seam vertices.
Parabidiminished rhombicosidodecahedron (Johnson solid J80): 10 triangles + 20 squares + 10 pentagons + 2 decagons. Two opposite pentagonal cupolas removed from the rhombicosidodecahedron.

Metabidiminished icosahedron (Johnson solid J62): 10 triangles + 2 pentagons. Two non-opposite pentagonal pyramids removed from the icosahedron (opposite removal gives the pentagonal antiprism instead).
Parabigyrate rhombicosidodecahedron (Johnson solid J73): the rhombicosidodecahedron with two opposite pentagonal cupolas each rotated 36° — same faces, two rings of 3.4.4.5 seam vertices.

Paragyrate diminished rhombicosidodecahedron (Johnson solid J77): one pentagonal cupola gyrated and one removed, in the PARA position. It shipped hedged as J77/J78 because the face and vertex census cannot separate the two; symmetry order can, and this one measures 10 (C_5v) against J78's 2 (C_s).
Diminished rhombicosidodecahedron (Johnson solid J76): 15 triangles + 25 squares + 11 pentagons + 1 decagon. One pentagonal cupola removed from the rhombicosidodecahedron.
Gyrate rhombicosidodecahedron (Johnson solid J72): the rhombicosidodecahedron with a single pentagonal cupola rotated 36° — same faces as the Archimedean solid, one ring of 3.4.4.5 seam vertices.

Square pyramid (Johnson solid J1): 4 triangles + 1 square. Inscribable, but its circumcentre sits in the base plane, so the square is a great circle and the spherical developer's polygon parameterisation ends exactly there.
Pentagonal pyramid (Johnson solid J2): 5 triangles + 1 pentagon. A cap of the icosahedron.
Triangular cupola (Johnson solid J3): 4 triangles + 3 squares + 1 hexagon. Half a cuboctahedron, cut on the hexagon.
Square cupola (Johnson solid J4): 4 triangles + 5 squares + 1 octagon. A cap of the rhombicuboctahedron.
Pentagonal cupola (Johnson solid J5): 5 triangles + 5 squares + 1 pentagon + 1 decagon. A cap of the rhombicosidodecahedron.
Elongated triangular bipyramid (Johnson solid J14): 6 triangles + 3 squares. A triangular prism capped at both ends; no circumsphere, so no spherical development exists.
Elongated square bipyramid (Johnson solid J15): 8 triangles + 4 squares. A cube capped at two opposite faces; no circumsphere.
Elongated pentagonal bipyramid (Johnson solid J16): 10 triangles + 5 squares. A pentagonal prism capped at both ends; no circumsphere.
Gyrobifastigium (Johnson solid J26): 4 triangles + 4 squares. Two triangular prisms joined square to square with a quarter turn; the only Johnson solid that tiles space. No circumsphere.
Square orthobicupola (Johnson solid J28): 8 triangles + 10 squares. Two square cupolas joined with LIKE faces meeting, which is what puts 3.3.4.4 at the equator. No circumsphere.
Square gyrobicupola (Johnson solid J29): 8 triangles + 10 squares. The same two cupolas given a 45-degree twist, so the equator alternates 3.4.3.4. No circumsphere.
Pentagonal orthobicupola (Johnson solid J30): 10 triangles + 10 squares + 2 pentagons. No circumsphere.
Pentagonal gyrobicupola (Johnson solid J31): 10 triangles + 10 squares + 2 pentagons, the twisted twin of J30. No circumsphere.

Elongated triangular orthobicupola (Johnson solid J35): 8 triangles + 12 squares. Two triangular cupolas with a hexagonal prism between them; ortho and gyro share a vertex configuration here and differ only by an equatorial mirror. No circumsphere.
Elongated triangular gyrobicupola (Johnson solid J36): 8 triangles + 12 squares, the twisted twin of J35. No circumsphere.
Elongated pentagonal orthobicupola (Johnson solid J38): 10 triangles + 20 squares + 2 pentagons. No circumsphere.
Elongated pentagonal gyrobicupola (Johnson solid J39): 10 triangles + 20 squares + 2 pentagons, the twisted twin of J38. No circumsphere.
Triaugmented hexagonal prism (Johnson solid J57): 12 triangles + 3 squares + 2 hexagons. A hexagonal prism with a square pyramid on each of its three alternating side faces. No circumsphere.

Pentagonal rotunda (Johnson solid J6): 10{3} + 6{5} + 1{10}, 20 vertices, 35 edges, 17 faces. Found by develop_euclid at k = 3 — three vertex orbits — which is the same exhaustive search that gave the 2-orbit Johnson solids, one orbit deeper. That it is one of the 92 is Zalgaller's theorem, not an inference from the census: a convex polyhedron with regular faces is Platonic, Archimedean, a prism, an antiprism or a Johnson solid, and none of those is uniform.

Non-convex regular-faced polyhedron: 10{3}, 7 vertices, 15 edges, 10 faces, 2 vertex orbits. It SELF-INTERSECTS — a face edge passes through the interior of a face it shares no vertex with, and it has no circumsphere — which is why the spherical developer could never see it, and why it took solving for dihedral angles in R3 to find. It ships unnamed: Johnson's 92 and Zalgaller's completeness proof are for CONVEX regular-faced polyhedra, past convexity only the 57 non-convex UNIFORM polyhedra are enumerated, and there is no catalogue a name could be checked against. This shelf is complete for up to 3 vertex orbits over regular {3,4,5,6,8,10}-gons, and only for solids whose every vertex has positive angular defect — a saddle vertex, where the angles sum past 360°, is outside what the search enumerates rather than something it missed.
